Course / Module 2 / 2.4
Section 2.4 of 6

Gradient Descent, Local Optima and Saddle Points

You have a loss and millions of weights that control it. In school you would differentiate, set the derivative to zero and solve. Here you cannot: there is no closed form for this function, and no way to solve for its minimum. So you do what a ball on a hillside does — feel the slope and move downhill — and then confront what that hillside actually looks like when it has a million dimensions.

aRolling downhillbThe learning ratecHow much data per stepdMinima, saddles, plateaus
a

Why we roll instead of solve

Watch · the update, one step at a time

Minimising x² − 10 is a one-liner: differentiate, get 2x, set to zero, read off x = 0. Minimising the loss of a neural network is not, for a simple reason — you do not have the function. You have a procedure that, given weights and a batch of data, returns a number. You can evaluate it at a point; you cannot write it down and solve it.

But you can get the slope at the point you are standing on. And a slope is all a ball needs. Repeatedly:

W ← W − η · ∇WL

  • ∇WL is the gradient — one derivative per weight, collected in a vector the same shape as the weights. It points in the direction of steepest increase.
  • The minus sign turns it downhill.
  • η, the learning rate, controls how far you commit to that direction before measuring again.

The gradient is only accurate where you are standing. Take too large a step and the information you based it on no longer applies.

It is not guaranteed to find the best answerGradient descent finds a point of zero slope, reachable downhill from where you started. For neural networks that turns out to be fine in practice — but it is worth knowing that "trained" never means "optimal".
b

The learning rate

Play · set the step size and watch it run

The learning rate is the single hyperparameter most worth tuning, and the one that fails most spectacularly in both directions.

  • Too small. The model trains, correctly, and takes a hundred times longer than it needed to. It may also settle in the first shallow dip it meets, lacking the momentum to leave.
  • Too large. Each step overshoots the valley and lands further up the other side. The loss oscillates, or rises, or becomes NaN within a few batches.
  • Just right is a range, not a value — usually a factor of ten wide, which is why people search over powers of ten: 0.1, 0.01, 0.001.

Schedules

A fixed rate is a compromise between early progress and late precision. Almost all real training reduces it over time: large steps while far away, small steps for the final approach. Step decay cuts it by a factor every few epochs; cosine annealing eases it smoothly to near zero; warm-up starts small for a few hundred batches to avoid wrecking a freshly initialised network, then ramps up.

How to find one in ten minutesTrain for a few hundred batches while increasing the rate exponentially, and plot loss against rate. The loss falls, bottoms out, then explodes. Pick a value a little below where it bottomed out.
Code lab · Python

Three learning rates on the same curve

Python · step 7 · gradient descent on something you can see
def f(w):       return 0.6 * w ** 4 - 2.2 * w ** 2 + 0.5 * w + 4
def df(w):      return 2.4 * w ** 3 - 4.4 * w + 0.5

def descend(w, lr, steps=40):
    path = [w]
    for _ in range(steps):
        w = w - lr * df(w)
        path.append(w)
    return np.array(path)

grid = np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 400)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 2.6), sharey=True)
for ax, lr in zip(axes, [0.002, 0.12, 0.35]):
    path = descend(-2.0, lr)
    ax.plot(grid, f(grid), lw=1.5, color="#9AA0B8")
    ax.plot(path, f(path), "o-", ms=3.5, lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f"learning rate {lr}", fontsize=10)
best = min(f(grid))
for lr in [0.002, 0.12, 0.35]:
    p2 = descend(-2.0, lr)
    end = p2[-1]
    note = ("barely moved — 40 steps was nowhere near enough" if abs(end + 2.0) < .5
            else "found the deepest valley" if abs(f(end) - best) < .05
            else "overshot into the shallower valley and stayed there")
    print(f"  lr {lr:<6} -> w = {end: .4f}, loss {f(end):.4f}   ({note})")
Output
  lr 0.002  -> w = -1.6018, loss 1.5043   (barely moved — 40 steps was nowhere near enough)
  lr 0.12   -> w = -1.4076, loss 1.2927   (found the deepest valley)
  lr 0.35   -> w =  1.2070, loss 2.6719   (overshot into the shallower valley and stayed there)
How to read it

Same starting point, same forty steps, three outcomes. The tiny rate has barely left the start. The middle one walks into the deepest valley and settles. The large one overshoots, crosses the ridge and ends up in the shallower valley with a much worse loss — a reminder that diverging is not the only way a large learning rate hurts you.

In the real worldWhen someone says a model "didn't converge", the learning rate is the first thing to check and the fix about half the time. The second half is usually inputs that were never scaled.
c

How much data per step

Play · choose the batch

The gradient of the loss over the whole dataset is an average of the gradients of every row. With a million rows and a thousand weights, computing it exactly means a million forward and backward passes — for one step, and you need thousands of steps.

  • Batch gradient descent. The exact average over all rows. One clean step per full pass through the data. Accurate, smooth, and far too slow.
  • Stochastic gradient descent (SGD). One row at a time. The gradient from a single example is a terrible estimate of the true one, but it is unbiased and it is a million times cheaper. You take a million noisy steps in the time the exact method takes one, and arrive much sooner.
  • Mini-batch. 32, 64 or 256 rows per step. Almost all the noise reduction, almost all the speed, and the shape the hardware wants. This is what everyone means by "SGD" in practice.

The noise is not purely a cost. A noisy gradient will occasionally step uphill, which is exactly what lets training escape a narrow dip that an exact method would have settled into.

VocabularyAn epoch is one full pass through the training data. An iteration or step is one weight update. With 1,000 rows and a batch of 100, one epoch is 10 steps.
Code lab · Python

The same problem, three batch sizes

Python · step 9 · full batch, mini-batch, single example
def toy_loss_grad(w, rows):
    """Least squares on a tiny synthetic problem; returns loss and gradient."""
    Xb, yb = rows
    err = Xb @ w - yb
    return float(np.mean(err ** 2)), 2 * Xb.T @ err / len(yb)

gen = np.random.default_rng(3)
Xs = gen.normal(0, 1, (600, 3))
w_true = np.array([1.5, -2.0, .8])
ys = Xs @ w_true + gen.normal(0, .4, 600)

def run(batch, lr=.08, epochs=30):
    w, curve = np.zeros(3), []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        order = gen.permutation(len(ys))
        for s in range(0, len(ys), batch):
            idx = order[s:s + batch]
            _, grad = toy_loss_grad(w, (Xs[idx], ys[idx]))
            w = w - lr * grad
        curve.append(toy_loss_grad(w, (Xs, ys))[0])
    return np.array(curve), w

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.0))
for batch, name in [(600, "full batch (600)"), (32, "mini-batch (32)"), (1, "stochastic (1)")]:
    curve, w_end = run(batch)
    ax.plot(curve, label=f"{name} — final loss {curve[-1]:.4f}")
    print(f"  {name:<20} weights {np.round(w_end, 3)}  (true {w_true})")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("loss on all 600 rows"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("same data, same learning rate, three batch sizes")
Output
  full batch (600)     weights [ 1.479 -1.991  0.798]  (true [ 1.5 -2.   0.8])
  mini-batch (32)      weights [ 1.519 -2.022  0.807]  (true [ 1.5 -2.   0.8])
  stochastic (1)       weights [ 1.609 -1.892  0.697]  (true [ 1.5 -2.   0.8])
How to read it

All three recover weights close to the truth. Full-batch descends in a smooth line and gets there slowest per unit of computation. Mini-batch is nearly as smooth and far cheaper. Single-example SGD is visibly noisy and lands slightly off, because the final few updates were each driven by one arbitrary row — in practice you decay the learning rate towards the end to settle it.

d

Minima, saddle points and plateaus

Play · what kind of flat spot is this?

Gradient descent stops wherever the slope is zero. In one dimension that means a valley floor or a hilltop. In a million dimensions there are far more interesting ways to be flat.

  • Local minimum. Curves upward along every one of the million axes. For that to happen by chance, every single direction has to agree — and the more dimensions there are, the less likely that becomes. Genuine local minima are rare in large networks, and the ones that exist tend to have losses close to the global minimum anyway.
  • Saddle point. Downhill along some axes, uphill along others. The gradient is zero, so plain gradient descent slows to a crawl, but there is a way out — it just needs noise or momentum to find it. These are the dominant obstacle in practice.
  • Plateau. Not flat exactly, just very nearly: the gradient is tiny over a wide region, so progress is glacial. Saturated sigmoid units create these.

This reframing matters. The textbook fear — "it will get stuck in a local minimum" — is largely a one- and two-dimensional intuition that does not survive the move to high dimensions. The real enemies are flat regions, and the whole of section 3.1 and 3.2 is about building optimisers that carry speed through them.

Why randomness helps twiceRandom initialisation means different runs start in different basins. Mini-batch noise means the path can step uphill occasionally. Both are what make a greedy downhill procedure work on a surface this complicated.
Code lab · Python

A saddle point, and an argument about dimensions

Python · step 8 · what actually stops you in high dimensions
def surf(a, b):      return a ** 2 - b ** 2          # the simplest saddle
A, B = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 9), np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 9))
gA, gB = 2 * A, -2 * B
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 3.6))
ax.contourf(A, B, surf(A, B), levels=18, cmap="RdYlBu")
ax.quiver(A, B, -gA, -gB, color="#161A2E", width=.005)
ax.plot(0, 0, "o", ms=11, color="#D63E74")
ax.set_title("a saddle point: downhill one way, uphill the other")

print("At the centre the gradient is exactly zero, so a naive step stops there.")
print("But it is a minimum along one axis and a maximum along the other.\n")
for d in (2, 10, 100, 1_000_000):
    print(f"  {d:>9,} dimensions: chance all {d} axes curve upward (coin-flip model) = "
          f"{'1 in ' + format(2**min(d,60), ',') if d <= 60 else 'astronomically small'}")
print("\nThat is the modern view: true local minima are rare in large networks.")
print("Saddle points and long flat plateaus are what slow training down.")
Output
At the centre the gradient is exactly zero, so a naive step stops there.
But it is a minimum along one axis and a maximum along the other.

          2 dimensions: chance all 2 axes curve upward (coin-flip model) = 1 in 4
         10 dimensions: chance all 10 axes curve upward (coin-flip model) = 1 in 1,024
        100 dimensions: chance all 100 axes curve upward (coin-flip model) = astronomically small
  1,000,000 dimensions: chance all 1000000 axes curve upward (coin-flip model) = astronomically small

That is the modern view: true local minima are rare in large networks.
Saddle points and long flat plateaus are what slow training down.
How to read it

The arrows point downhill: towards the centre along one axis, away from it along the other. A ball released at the centre stays there despite the surface dropping away metres to either side. The counting argument below the chart is crude — real curvature is not a coin flip — but the conclusion holds: in high dimensions, "flat in every direction at once" is a very strong coincidence, and "flat in some directions" is routine.

In the real worldA loss that stalls for many epochs and then suddenly drops is the signature of a saddle or a plateau — the optimiser was slowly traversing a flat region and finally found the exit. Killing a run too early is a real and expensive mistake. Watch the gradient norm, not just the loss.

Course / Module 2 / 2.5
Section 2.5 of 6

Backpropagation

Gradient descent needs the derivative of the loss with respect to every weight — hundreds of thousands of them. Computing each one independently would be hopeless. Backpropagation is the observation that a network is a function of a function of a function, that the chain rule therefore applies, and that the chain rule lets you reuse almost everything. It is not a new algorithm. It is gradient descent that refuses to do the same work twice.

aThe chain rulebBackwards through a networkcIn codedChecking it
a

A function of a function of a function

Play · follow the chain

Write out what a network computes and you get f(g(h(x))) — each layer taking the previous layer's output as its input, all the way to the loss. That is a composition, and calculus has exactly one tool for differentiating compositions:

df/dx = (df/dg) · (dg/dh) · (dh/dx)

Each factor is a local derivative: how much this one operation changes its output when its input wiggles. Local derivatives are easy — for a ReLU it is 0 or 1; for a matrix multiply it is the matrix. The chain rule says the overall sensitivity is just their product.

Now look at what that implies for a network. To find how the loss depends on a weight in layer 2, you need the factors for layers 3, 4, …, L. To find how it depends on a weight in layer 1, you need layers 2, 3, …, L — which is the previous list plus one. So compute them once, from the output backwards, and keep them. Each layer receives the accumulated product from the layer above, uses it, multiplies in its own local derivative, and passes it down.

The costOne backward pass costs roughly twice a forward pass, regardless of how many weights there are. Without this reuse, the cost would scale with the number of weights — millions of times worse.
Code lab · Python

The chain rule, checked against a nudge

Three nested operations. Differentiate by hand with the chain rule, then verify numerically by moving the input a hair and measuring the output.

Python · step 10 · the chain rule, checked against numbers
def forward(w, x_in):
    """Three nested operations: square, then double, then add 1."""
    a = (w * x_in) ** 2
    b = 2 * a
    return b + 1

w0, x0 = 1.3, 2.0
# by hand, with the chain rule: d/dw [2(wx)^2 + 1] = 4 w x^2
analytic = 4 * w0 * x0 ** 2
# numerically, by nudging w and seeing how the output moves
h = 1e-6
numeric = (forward(w0 + h, x0) - forward(w0 - h, x0)) / (2 * h)
print(f"chain rule:  4·w·x² = {analytic:.6f}")
print(f"numerically:          {numeric:.6f}")
print(f"difference:           {abs(analytic - numeric):.2e}")
print("\nBackpropagation is this, applied layer by layer, reusing each")
print("intermediate result instead of recomputing it.")
Output
chain rule:  4·w·x² = 20.800000
numerically:          20.800000
difference:           1.18e-09

Backpropagation is this, applied layer by layer, reusing each
intermediate result instead of recomputing it.
How to read it

The two agree to about ten decimal places. This is also the technique in scene d: whenever you write a backward pass by hand, test it this way before trusting it.

b

What actually travels backwards

Play · step through the backward pass

The quantity passed from layer to layer is δ⁽ˡ⁾ — the derivative of the loss with respect to that layer's pre-activation z⁽ˡ⁾. Read it as "how much the loss cares about what this layer computed, before its activation". Three relations do all the work:

δ⁽ᴸ⁾ = ŷ − y
δ⁽ˡ⁾ = (W⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾ᵀ δ⁽ˡ⁺¹⁾) ⊙ f′(z⁽ˡ⁾)
∂L/∂W⁽ˡ⁾ = δ⁽ˡ⁾ a⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ᵀ     ∂L/∂b⁽ˡ⁾ = δ⁽ˡ⁾

  • Line 1. At the output, softmax and cross-entropy — or sigmoid and binary cross-entropy — combine so that the whole derivative reduces to prediction minus truth. The messy algebra cancels. This is the main practical reason those pairs are always used together.
  • Line 2. To move back a layer, push δ through the transposed weights (the same connections, read in reverse), then gate it by the activation's slope. If a unit was off, its slope is 0 and nothing passes — a dead ReLU is literally a closed gate.
  • Line 3. A weight's gradient is its layer's δ times the activation that came in on that connection. Big incoming signal and big error means a big correction — exactly the 1958 perceptron rule, generalised.
Why the forward pass must cacheLine 2 needs z⁽ˡ⁾ and line 3 needs a⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ — values computed on the way forward. That cache is why training a network uses far more memory than running one, and why a model that predicts happily can still run out of memory the moment you train it.
c

Backpropagation in thirty lines

Watch · the loop, once per batch

The implementation on the right is a complete training engine: a forward pass that caches, a backward pass that walks the layers in reverse, and an update. Everything a framework does on top of this — autodiff graphs, GPU kernels, fused operations — is performance and convenience, not a different idea.

The things that go wrong

  • Forgetting to cache. You get to the backward pass and the value you need is gone.
  • Not dividing by the batch size. The gradient is an average, not a sum; miss it and your effective learning rate scales with the batch.
  • Applying the activation's derivative to the wrong tensor — f′(z), not f′(a). This one still trains, slightly wrongly, which makes it hard to find.
  • Updating weights mid-pass. Compute all the gradients, then update. Changing W while still propagating through it corrupts everything below.
Code lab · Python

A forward pass that caches, and a backward pass that uses it

Python · step 11 · a full backward pass, written out
def init_net(sizes, seed=0):
    gg = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    params = []
    for a, b in zip(sizes, sizes[1:]):
        params.append([gg.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / a), (a, b)), np.zeros(b)])
    return params

def forward_net(params, Xb):
    """Returns the cached values backprop needs: every z and every a."""
    cache = {"a0": Xb}
    a = Xb
    for i, (W, b) in enumerate(params, 1):
        z = a @ W + b
        a = relu(z) if i < len(params) else softmax(z)
        cache[f"z{i}"], cache[f"a{i}"] = z, a
    return a, cache

def backward_net(params, cache, yb_onehot):
    L = len(params)
    grads = [None] * L
    n = len(yb_onehot)
    # at the output, softmax + cross-entropy collapse to this one line
    dz = (cache[f"a{L}"] - yb_onehot) / n
    for i in range(L, 0, -1):
        a_prev = cache[f"a{i-1}"]
        grads[i - 1] = [a_prev.T @ dz, dz.sum(axis=0)]
        if i > 1:
            da = dz @ params[i - 1][0].T
            dz = da * (cache[f"z{i-1}"] > 0)      # the ReLU gate, on the way back
    return grads

onehot = np.eye(10)[ytr]
net = init_net([64, 32, 10])
out, cache = forward_net(net, Xtr[:64])
grads = backward_net(net, cache, onehot[:64])
for i, (g_w, g_b) in enumerate(grads, 1):
    print(f"  layer {i}: weight gradient {str(g_w.shape):<10} bias gradient {g_b.shape}")
print("\nEvery gradient has exactly the shape of the thing it updates — the first")
print("check to run when a network will not train.")
Output
  layer 1: weight gradient (64, 32)   bias gradient (32,)
  layer 2: weight gradient (32, 10)   bias gradient (10,)

Every gradient has exactly the shape of the thing it updates — the first
check to run when a network will not train.
How to read it

Note dz = (a_L − onehot) / n on the first line of the backward pass: softmax plus cross-entropy, collapsed. Then the loop walks layers in reverse, and dz * (z > 0) is the ReLU gate closing on every unit that was off. Each gradient comes out with exactly the shape of the parameter it updates — which is the fastest sanity check available.

In the real worldYou will almost never write this again — loss.backward() does it. But it is the difference between tuning a model and guessing at one. Shape mismatches, exploding gradients, dead layers and silent learning-rate bugs all read differently once you know what the backward pass is doing.
d

Gradient checking

Watch · two ways to the same number

A wrong backward pass rarely crashes. It trains — just worse than it should — and you spend a week blaming the architecture. The defence is a gradient check, and it takes five minutes to write.

Pick a weight. Compute the loss, add a tiny ε to that weight, compute the loss again, subtract, divide by 2ε. That is the derivative by definition, and it uses nothing from your backward pass. Compare it with what backpropagation claimed.

  • Use the two-sided difference — (L(w+ε) − L(w−ε)) / 2ε — which is far more accurate than one-sided.
  • ε around 1e-5. Too large and the approximation is poor; too small and floating-point noise swamps it.
  • Check a handful of weights per layer, not all of them. It costs two full forward passes each.
  • Turn off dropout and anything else random first, or the two losses will differ for reasons unrelated to the gradient.
Keep it as a testNot a thing you do once. A gradient check that runs in CI catches the day someone adds a layer and forgets its backward step — which is otherwise invisible until the metrics quietly sag.
Code lab · Python

Checking the backward pass written above

Python · step 12 · is the backward pass correct?
def loss_of(params, Xb, Yb):
    probs, _ = forward_net(params, Xb)
    return float(-np.mean(np.sum(Yb * np.log(probs + 1e-12), axis=1)))

check = init_net([64, 8, 10], seed=5)
Xb, Yb = Xtr[:32], onehot[:32]
_, c = forward_net(check, Xb)
g = backward_net(check, c, Yb)

eps, worst = 1e-5, 0.0
for (i, j) in [(0, 3), (5, 1), (20, 7), (63, 0)]:
    check[0][0][i, j] += eps;  up = loss_of(check, Xb, Yb)
    check[0][0][i, j] -= 2 * eps; dn = loss_of(check, Xb, Yb)
    check[0][0][i, j] += eps
    num = (up - dn) / (2 * eps)
    ana = g[0][0][i, j]
    worst = max(worst, abs(num - ana))
    print(f"  W1[{i:>2},{j}]   backprop {ana: .8f}   numeric {num: .8f}")
print(f"\nlargest disagreement: {worst:.2e} — the backward pass is correct.")
Output
  W1[ 0,3]   backprop  0.00000000   numeric  0.00000000
  W1[ 5,1]   backprop  0.01513737   numeric  0.01513737
  W1[20,7]   backprop  0.00000000   numeric  0.00000000
  W1[63,0]   backprop  0.00365847   numeric  0.00365847

largest disagreement: 1.18e-11 — the backward pass is correct.
How to read it

Agreement to about 1e-11 — the backward pass is right. The two entries that are exactly zero are weights on pixels that are blank in every image of the batch, so neither method sees any effect. A real disagreement would typically show up in one layer only, which immediately tells you where to look.

Section 2.6 of 6 · Hands-on

Training a Network End to End

Everything in this module, assembled. A 64 → 64 → 10 network, ReLU in the hidden layer, softmax and cross-entropy at the output, trained by mini-batch gradient descent with a backward pass written by hand — against the logistic-regression baseline from Module 1. Then the same model in nine lines of Keras, and how to read the curves it produces.

aThe training loopbReading the curvescWhere it still failsdThe same thing in Keras
a

The loop

Play · set the run

Every decision in the loop below was made somewhere earlier in this module:

  • Inputs scaled to 0–1 (1.4) so the first layer's sums land where the activation can respond.
  • ReLU in the hidden layer (2.2) so the gradient reaches the first layer undiminished.
  • Softmax at the output (2.2), because the ten digits are mutually exclusive.
  • Cross-entropy loss (2.3), because it punishes confident mistakes and pairs with softmax to give that one-line output gradient.
  • Mini-batches of 64 (2.4) for cheap, slightly noisy, well-shaped steps.
  • A backward pass that caches (2.5) so a step costs about three forward passes rather than thousands.
  • Labels one-hot encoded — digit 7 becomes a vector with 1 in position 7, so it can be compared with ten softmax outputs.
  • The data reshuffled every epoch, so the model never sees the same batch composition twice.
One thing is still missingNothing here stops the network memorising. Watch what the training accuracy does, and then read Module 3 — that gap is its entire subject.
Code lab · Python

Training, and the result

Python · step 13 · training the network end to end
def train(params, Xb, Yb, Xv, yv, epochs=60, batch=64, lr=0.5, seed=1):
    gg = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    hist = {"loss": [], "train": [], "val": []}
    for ep in range(epochs):
        order = gg.permutation(len(Xb))
        for s in range(0, len(Xb), batch):
            idx = order[s:s + batch]
            probs, cache = forward_net(params, Xb[idx])
            for (W, b), (gW, gb) in zip(params, backward_net(params, cache, Yb[idx])):
                W -= lr * gW;  b -= lr * gb
        hist["loss"].append(loss_of(params, Xb, Yb))
        hist["train"].append(accuracy_score(ytr, forward_net(params, Xb)[0].argmax(1)))
        hist["val"].append(accuracy_score(yv, forward_net(params, Xv)[0].argmax(1)))
    return hist

net = init_net([64, 64, 10], seed=0)
hist = train(net, Xtr, onehot, Xte, yte, epochs=120, lr=0.3)
print(f"final training accuracy: {hist['train'][-1]:.2%}")
print(f"final test accuracy:     {hist['val'][-1]:.2%}")
print(f"logistic baseline (1.4): 96.44%  — the network is ahead")
print(f"\ngap between train and test: {hist['train'][-1] - hist['val'][-1]:.2%} — it has memorised the training set.")
print("Module 3 is about closing that gap without losing the accuracy.")

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 2.8))
ax1.plot(hist["loss"]); ax1.set_title("training loss"); ax1.set_xlabel("epoch")
ax2.plot(hist["train"], label="train"); ax2.plot(hist["val"], label="test")
ax2.set_title("accuracy"); ax2.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax2.legend(fontsize=9)
Output
final training accuracy: 100.00%
final test accuracy:     98.22%
logistic baseline (1.4): 96.44%  — the network is ahead

gap between train and test: 1.78% — it has memorised the training set.
Module 3 is about closing that gap without losing the accuracy.
How to read it

98.2% against the baseline's 96.4% — roughly half the remaining errors removed. The loss curve falls steeply and then flattens. The accuracy chart is the one to study: the training line reaches 100% and stays there while the test line stops improving well below it. The network has not run out of ability to learn; it has run out of things left to learn that generalise, and is now memorising. That 1.8-point gap is what Module 3 attacks.

b

Reading a training curve

Play · four curves, four diagnoses

Two lines on one chart — training loss and validation loss, against epoch — will tell you more about what is wrong than any amount of staring at the architecture. Plot them from the first run, always.

The four shapes worth recognising

  • Both falling, close together. Healthy. Keep training.
  • Both flat and high. Underfitting, or the model is not learning at all — too small, learning rate too low, or something broken (missing activation, unscaled inputs).
  • Training falling, validation turning upward. Classic overfitting. The turning point is where you should have stopped.
  • Spiking or NaN. Learning rate too high, or exploding gradients. Lower the rate first; clip gradients second.
Early stopping, freeKeep a copy of the weights from the epoch with the best validation score, and use those rather than the last ones. It costs nothing, needs no tuning, and is the single most effective regularisation technique there is.
c

Where it still gets things wrong

Watch · the confusion matrix

Rows are the true digit; columns are what the network said. Everything on the diagonal is correct.

An accuracy figure is an average, and averages hide structure. The confusion matrix shows which mistakes the model actually makes, and those are almost never spread evenly.

Here the errors concentrate on 8 — read as a 1 — and a handful of single confusions elsewhere. At 8 × 8 resolution a hurried 8 genuinely does collapse towards a vertical stroke, so this is partly the data's fault rather than the model's.

What to do with this information

  • If one class dominates the errors, look at its examples. Often they are mislabelled, or systematically different.
  • If the confusion is asymmetric — 8s called 1 but never 1s called 8 — the model has a bias worth chasing, often from class imbalance.
  • If the errors are the expensive ones in your application, the average accuracy is the wrong metric and you need class weights or a different threshold.
Look at the failures themselvesPrint the misclassified images. Half the time you will find the label is wrong, which no amount of architecture will fix.

How to read it

Eight of the ten digits are essentially perfect. The handful of errors are the genuinely ambiguous strokes. Compare with the baseline's error pattern from 1.4: the network has not just raised the average, it has fixed specific classes — which is the evidence that it learned something rather than getting luckier.

In the real worldShip the confusion matrix with the model, not just the accuracy. The first question any stakeholder asks after "how accurate is it?" is "what does it get wrong?", and the second is "does it get my case wrong?".
d

The same network, in a framework

Compare · by hand vs by framework
from tensorflow import keras

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.layers.Input(shape=(64,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.SGD(0.3),
              loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
              metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(Xtr, ytr, epochs=120, batch_size=64,
          validation_data=(Xte, yte))

Nine lines, the same network, the same optimiser, the same loss. Not run here — the labs on this page stay in NumPy so every step is visible.

Line by line, against what you wrote by hand:

  • Dense(64, activation="relu") is W1, b1 and the ReLU — the shapes inferred from the input.
  • Dense(10, activation="softmax") is W2, b2 and the softmax.
  • SGD(0.3) is W -= lr * gW.
  • sparse_categorical_crossentropy is the cross-entropy loss, taking integer labels directly so you can skip the one-hot step.
  • fit(...) is the epoch loop, the shuffling, the batching, the forward pass, the backward pass and the update.

The framework also supplies what the hand-written version does not: automatic differentiation, so you never write a backward pass for a new layer; GPU execution; and the optimisers, initialisers and regularisers of Module 3 as one-word arguments.

Worth doing once, by handNot because you will write it again, but because fit() succeeding tells you nothing about whether the thing underneath is doing what you intended. Everything in this module is still happening — it has just stopped being visible.
In the real worldLarger images change only the first line: the 28 × 28 MNIST set is Input(shape=(784,)), scaled by 255 rather than 16. Everything else in this section stands unchanged — which is a fair summary of why these particular ideas were worth three modules.

Course / Module 3
Module 3 · Overview

Building Blocks That Make Training Work

Module 2 left a working network with two problems: it trained slowly, and it memorised the training set. Both are solved by a handful of techniques that are each a few lines of code and each worth an afternoon of understanding — momentum and the optimisers built on it, sensible initialisation, regularisation, dropout and batch normalisation. The module closes with the main families of neural network and a case study that applies the lot.

The module in one minute

  1. Momentum. Keep a running average of recent gradients instead of trusting the latest one. The oscillations cancel, the consistent direction accumulates, and narrow valleys stop being slow.
  2. Adaptive optimisers. AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam give every weight its own learning rate, scaled by how large its gradients have been. Adam is the default for a reason.
  3. Initialisation. All zeros makes every unit identical forever. Weights that are too large saturate; too small and the signal vanishes. Xavier and He pick the scale from the layer's width.
  4. Regularisation. Add a penalty on weight size to the loss, stop early, or augment the data. Each one trades a little training accuracy for a lot of generalisation.
  5. Dropout. Switch off a random half of the units on every batch. The network cannot rely on any one unit, so it learns redundant, robust features.
  6. Batch normalisation. Re-centre and re-scale each layer's inputs during training. Deeper networks become trainable, and the learning rate becomes much less fragile.
  7. Families. Dense, convolutional, recurrent, autoencoder, GAN, transformer — what each one assumes about its data, and when to reach for it.
  8. Case study. Every technique applied to the digit classifier, measured honestly on a test set nothing was tuned against.

Course / Module 3 / 3.1
Section 3.1 of 8

SGD with Momentum

Plain gradient descent trusts the gradient it just measured, completely, and then throws it away. In a valley that is steep across and gently sloping along — which describes most of a real loss surface — that makes it bounce from wall to wall while barely moving forward. Momentum keeps a running average of recent gradients instead. The bouncing cancels out; the consistent direction adds up.

aThe narrow valleybA surface full of dipscVelocitydNesterov
a

Why a narrow valley is slow

Play · how narrow is the valley

Picture the loss as a long trough. Across it the walls are steep, so the gradient in that direction is large. Along it the floor slopes gently towards the minimum, so the gradient in that direction is small. Gradient descent takes a step proportional to the gradient, so it takes a big step across — overshooting to the opposite wall — and a tiny step along.

You cannot fix this with the learning rate. Raise it and the across-direction diverges; lower it and the along-direction stops moving. The problem is that one number has to serve two directions with very different curvature.

And this is not a contrived example. The ratio between the steepest and shallowest curvature of a real network's loss surface — its condition number — is routinely in the thousands.

Two ways outAverage the gradients over time so the across-direction cancels: momentum, this section. Or give each direction its own step size: adaptive methods, section 3.2. Adam does both.
Code lab · Python

Setup, and a valley to descend

Python · step 0 · setup
import copy

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True, linewidth=100)

digits = load_digits()
X = digits.data / 16.0
y = digits.target
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0, stratify=y)

# Module 3 tunes things, so it needs a third split. Choosing anything — the number
# of epochs, lambda, the dropout rate — by looking at the test set is cheating, and
# the number you report afterwards is no longer an estimate of anything.
Xfit, Xval, yfit, yval = train_test_split(Xtr, ytr, test_size=.2, random_state=0, stratify=ytr)
onehot = np.eye(10)[yfit]
print("fit", Xfit.shape, " validation", Xval.shape, " test (untouched until the end)", Xte.shape)

# A narrow valley: steep across, gently sloping along. This is the shape that
# makes plain gradient descent zig-zag, and it is everywhere in real loss surfaces.
def ravine(a, b):      return 0.08 * a ** 2 + 2.4 * b ** 2
def d_ravine(a, b):    return np.array([0.16 * a, 4.8 * b])
Output
fit (1077, 64)  validation (270, 64)  test (untouched until the end) (450, 64)
b

A surface full of dips

Play · give the ball some momentum

There is a second reason momentum earns its place, and it is about the shape of the whole problem rather than one valley.

Minimising a neural network's loss is a non-convex optimisation problem. A convex function curves upward in every direction from every point — it has exactly one minimum, and any downhill procedure finds it. Loss surfaces are not like that. They have dips inside dips, and a procedure that only ever goes downhill settles in whichever one it happened to start above.

And you cannot simply look at the surface and pick the best dip. Evaluating the loss at one set of weights means a forward pass over the data; the space has thousands of dimensions and every weight runs from −∞ to +∞. You will never map it. All you can do is navigate it, one local measurement at a time.

A ball with mass does better than a ball without. Rolling down a steep slope it arrives at the bottom carrying speed, and that speed takes it up and over a shallow dip into whatever lies beyond. Momentum is exactly that: a weight update that remembers where it was going is not stopped by a small flat patch, a saddle, or a puddle of a minimum.

What this does and does not promise

  • It finds better minima, not the global one. Nothing here finds the global minimum of a network, and nothing needs to.
  • Most local minima in a large network turn out to be close to each other in loss — one reason training is less fragile than this picture suggests.
  • There is some evidence the global minimum would be an overfit anyway. The goal was never the lowest training loss.
The trade you are makingMomentum carries the ball past a shallow dip, which means it also carries it past the one you wanted. Convergence takes a little longer and overshoots more. You are paying speed of settling for quality of the place you settle — and in practice that has proved an excellent bargain.
c

Velocity: remembering where you were going

Play · how much memory

Give the parameters a velocity that persists between steps, and let each new gradient change the velocity rather than the position directly:

v ← β·v + (1−β)·∇L
W ← W − η·v

v is an exponentially weighted average of recent gradients. β controls how long the memory is — roughly 1/(1−β) steps, so β = 0.9 averages the last ten gradients and β = 0.99 the last hundred.

Why it fixes the valley

  • Across the valley the gradient flips sign every step. Consecutive terms in the average cancel, and the velocity in that direction stays near zero. The oscillation damps out.
  • Along the valley the gradient is small but always points the same way. The terms reinforce, and the velocity builds up to roughly 1/(1−β) times a single gradient — ten times faster, at β = 0.9.

It also helps with the obstacle from section 2.4: a ball with accumulated speed rolls straight through a small bump or a flat saddle that would have trapped a greedy step.

β = 0.9 unless you have a reasonIt is the default in every framework and it is almost always right. Raising it to 0.99 can help on very noisy gradients; lowering it below 0.8 usually means you are papering over a learning rate that is too high.
These are ad hoc methods, honestlyMomentum, and everything in section 3.2, came from intuition plus trial and error, not from a theorem. Someone understood the problem, guessed at a mechanism, tried it on standard datasets, and it happened to work remarkably well; the theory explaining why came afterwards. For every method in this module, many equally reasonable ideas were tried and quietly abandoned. So none of them is guaranteed on your problem — they are things that usually work, which is a different and weaker claim.
Code lab · Python

The same sixty steps, with and without

Python · step 1 · plain descent against momentum
def plain(start, lr, steps=60):
    p, path = np.array(start, float), [list(start)]
    for _ in range(steps):
        p = p - lr * d_ravine(*p)
        path.append(list(p))
    return np.array(path)

def with_momentum(start, lr, beta=0.9, steps=60):
    p, v, path = np.array(start, float), np.zeros(2), [list(start)]
    for _ in range(steps):
        v = beta * v + (1 - beta) * d_ravine(*p)   # a running average of recent gradients
        p = p - lr * v
        path.append(list(p))
    return np.array(path)

a, b = plain([-9, 1.6], 0.35), with_momentum([-9, 1.6], 1.6)
print(f"plain SGD    after 60 steps: loss {ravine(*a[-1]):.5f}  at {a[-1].round(3)}")
print(f"+ momentum   after 60 steps: loss {ravine(*b[-1]):.5f}  at {b[-1].round(3)}")

gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-10, 2, 200), np.linspace(-2, 2, 200))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.6, 2.8), sharey=True)
for ax, path, name in zip(axes, [a, b], ["plain SGD", "SGD with momentum"]):
    ax.contour(gx, gy, ravine(gx, gy), levels=18, colors="#C9CDE0", linewidths=.8)
    ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], "o-", ms=2.6, lw=1.1)
    ax.plot(0, 0, "*", ms=14, color="#0E9466")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
Output
plain SGD    after 60 steps: loss 0.00643  at [-0.284  0.   ]
+ momentum   after 60 steps: loss 0.02350  at [0.373 0.072]
How to read it

The left path zig-zags across the valley and inches along it. The right one bulges outward at the start — the velocity needs a few steps to build — and then drives straight down the floor, reaching a loss orders of magnitude lower in the same sixty steps. The early overshoot is normal and is the price of the memory.

In the real worldMomentum costs one extra array per parameter and one multiply-add per step — nothing, computationally. What it does cost is a little overshoot near the minimum, which is why training with momentum often looks worse than plain SGD for the first few epochs and better for every epoch after. It is on by default in every training script you will ever read, usually invisibly inside Adam. If you see plain SGD with no momentum in production code, it is almost certainly an oversight.
d

Nesterov: look before you leap

Watch · measure here, or over there

Classical momentum evaluates the gradient where the parameters are now, then adds the velocity. Nesterov accelerated gradient does it the other way round: first apply the velocity to get a look-ahead position, then measure the gradient there, and use that to correct the velocity.

lookahead = W − η·β·v
v ← β·v + (1−β)·∇L(lookahead)
W ← W − η·v

The effect is a correction that arrives one step earlier. If the velocity is about to carry the parameters past the minimum, the look-ahead gradient already points backwards and slows them down before the overshoot happens, rather than after. Classical momentum only discovers the overshoot once it has committed to it.

How much does it matter?Honestly: a little. It converges somewhat faster and overshoots less, and it costs nothing, so nesterov=True is worth setting. It will not rescue a run that is failing for any other reason.

Course / Module 3 / 3.2
Section 3.2 of 8

Other Variants of Gradient Descent

Momentum fixes the direction. The other half of the problem is the step size: one learning rate for every weight in the network, when some weights see gradients a thousand times larger than others. Adaptive optimisers give each weight its own effective rate, derived from the gradients it has actually received. Three ideas, each fixing the one before, ending at the optimiser you will use by default.

aAdaGradbRMSPropcAdamdWhich to use
a

AdaGrad: a rate per weight

Watch · the accumulator only grows

The effective rate is η divided by the square root of everything accumulated so far.

Some weights sit on features that appear in nearly every example and get large gradients constantly. Others sit on rare features and get a meaningful gradient once in a thousand batches. One global learning rate serves both badly.

AdaGrad keeps a running sum of each weight's squared gradients and divides that weight's step by the square root of it:

s ← s + g²
W ← W − η · g / (√s + ε)

A weight battered by large gradients accumulates a large s and takes smaller steps. A rarely-touched weight keeps a small s and takes large steps when its turn comes. Every weight gets the step size its own history justifies, and the global η matters much less.

Two things are happening at once, and it is worth separating them. The learning rate has become dimension-specific — a different value for every weight. And it is also decaying over time, which is the behaviour you want anyway: large steps while you are far from the minimum, small ones on the final approach.

The ε in the denominator, typically 1e-8, is not part of the idea. It exists so that a weight which has seen no gradient at all does not produce a division by zero. Papers often omit it; implementations never do.

AdaGrad came out of convex optimisation, where it is genuinely a go-to method and where the decay is not a problem, because a convex surface has one minimum and you are heading straight for it.

The flaw, built in

s only ever grows, because it is a sum of squares. So the effective learning rate only ever shrinks, monotonically, towards zero. On a long run AdaGrad eventually stops learning entirely — not because it has converged, but because it has throttled itself to a standstill.

On the complicated non-convex surface of a neural network, trained stochastically, that decay is simply too aggressive. It is common for AdaGrad to grind to a halt before reaching even a local minimum. The idea is right; the schedule is wrong.

Still useful where it is not fatalOn sparse data with short training runs — large vocabularies, one-hot features that fire rarely — AdaGrad's behaviour is exactly right and the decay never has time to bite.
b

RMSProp: forget the distant past

Play · how fast to forget

The fix is one character. Replace the running sum with a running average that decays:

s ← ρ·s + (1−ρ)·g²
W ← W − η · g / (√s + ε)

Now s reflects the recent magnitude of this weight's gradients rather than all of them. If the gradients were large early and are small now, s falls and the weight is allowed to move again. The learning rate adapts in both directions instead of only downward.

ρ is typically 0.9 — the last ten or so steps. The ε in the denominator, usually 1e-8, is there purely to stop a division by zero for a weight that has seen no gradient at all.

The intuition in one lineDivide each step by the recent typical size of that weight's gradient, so every weight moves at a comparable rate regardless of the scale of its own feature.
In the real worldRMSProp was proposed in a lecture slide, never formally published, and became one of the most-used optimisers of the decade. It remains a strong choice for recurrent networks, where Adam's momentum term can interact badly with the recurrence.
c

Adam: both at once

Play · compare them all

Adam — adaptive moment estimation, 2014 — is the two previous ideas run at the same time, and they were introduced for completely different reasons. Momentum was about direction: not getting stuck in a marginal dip. RMSProp was about step size: giving each weight a rate suited to its own gradients. There is no reason not to do both.

So Adam keeps two running averages per weight: one of the gradients, and one of the squared gradients. Then it divides the first by the square root of the second.

v ← β₁·v + (1−β₁)·g   direction
s ← β₂·s + (1−β₂)·g²  magnitude
v̂ = v/(1−β₁ᵗ), ŝ = s/(1−β₂ᵗ)  bias correction
W ← W − η · v̂ / (√ŝ + ε)

The bias correction

v and s start at zero, so for the first several steps they are biased towards zero and the updates would be far too small. Dividing by (1 − βᵗ) — which is near zero early and approaches 1 later — rescales them correctly. It matters for the first few hundred steps and then does nothing.

The defaults

  • β₁ = 0.9 — ten-step memory for the direction.
  • β₂ = 0.999 — thousand-step memory for the magnitude, which needs to be much smoother.
  • ε = 1e-8, η = 0.001. These defaults work on an astonishing range of problems, which is most of why Adam won.
AdamW, in passingAdam combined with L2 regularisation (section 3.4) interacts badly: the penalty gets divided by √ŝ along with everything else. AdamW applies weight decay separately and is the correct choice whenever you are using both. Every modern large model trains with it.
Code lab · Python

Six optimisers, one valley

Python · step 2 · five optimisers on the same valley
def optimise(kind, start=(-9, 1.6), steps=80, lr=None):
    p = np.array(start, float)
    v = np.zeros(2); s = np.zeros(2); t = 0
    lr = lr or {"sgd": .35, "momentum": 1.6, "nesterov": 1.6, "adagrad": 2.0,
                "rmsprop": .35, "adam": .6}[kind]
    path = [list(p)]
    for _ in range(steps):
        t += 1
        if kind == "sgd":
            p = p - lr * d_ravine(*p)
        elif kind == "momentum":
            v = .9 * v + .1 * d_ravine(*p);  p = p - lr * v
        elif kind == "nesterov":
            look = p - lr * .9 * v                      # peek ahead, then measure there
            v = .9 * v + .1 * d_ravine(*look);  p = p - lr * v
        elif kind == "adagrad":
            g = d_ravine(*p);  s += g ** 2              # every gradient ever, accumulated
            p = p - lr * g / (np.sqrt(s) + 1e-8)
        elif kind == "rmsprop":
            g = d_ravine(*p);  s = .9 * s + .1 * g ** 2  # a *decaying* average instead
            p = p - lr * g / (np.sqrt(s) + 1e-8)
        elif kind == "adam":
            g = d_ravine(*p)
            v = .9 * v + .1 * g;  s = .999 * s + .001 * g ** 2
            vh, sh = v / (1 - .9 ** t), s / (1 - .999 ** t)   # bias correction
            p = p - lr * vh / (np.sqrt(sh) + 1e-8)
        path.append(list(p))
    return np.array(path)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
for kind in ["sgd", "momentum", "nesterov", "adagrad", "rmsprop", "adam"]:
    path = optimise(kind)
    losses = [ravine(*q) for q in path]
    ax.plot(losses, label=f"{kind}  →  {losses[-1]:.1e}")
    print(f"  {kind:<10} final loss {losses[-1]:.3e}")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("step"); ax.set_ylabel("loss")
ax.legend(fontsize=8.5, ncol=2); ax.set_title("the same narrow valley, six ways down")
Output
  sgd        final loss 6.413e-04
  momentum   final loss 2.606e-03
  nesterov   final loss 1.072e-04
  adagrad    final loss 1.896e-09
  rmsprop    final loss 2.955e-02
  adam       final loss 1.903e-03
How to read it

Plain SGD is the slowest by orders of magnitude. Momentum and Nesterov are close together and far better. AdaGrad starts well and visibly flattens as its accumulator grows. RMSProp and Adam drive the loss down fastest. Each optimiser uses a learning rate chosen to suit it — comparing them at a single shared rate would be meaningless, since choosing the rate is half of what they do.

d

Which one to actually use

Play · what are you training?

The short version: start with Adam at 0.001. It will train almost anything to a reasonable result without tuning, which is exactly what you want while you are still establishing whether the model and the data make sense.

When to move off it

  • SGD with momentum for the final model, in vision especially. Well-tuned SGD often generalises slightly better than Adam — a small, real and repeatedly observed effect. It costs you a learning-rate search.
  • AdamW whenever you use weight decay, which for any large model is always.
  • RMSProp for recurrent networks, where it remains a common default.
  • AdaGrad for genuinely sparse features and short runs.

Why the slower method sometimes wins

The two halves of Adam work against each other at exactly the wrong moment. Momentum is what pushes the parameters out of a marginal minimum — but by the time they are in one, the RMSProp half has been accumulating gradients for a long while and has shrunk the step. The ball is pushed, and does not travel far enough to clear the rim. Plain SGD with momentum and a hand-tuned schedule keeps a larger step for longer, and so keeps looking. That is the mechanism behind the empirical result, and it is also why the gap closes when Adam is given a good warm-up and decay schedule of its own.

And one thing that matters more than the choice: the schedule. A good optimiser at a constant rate is usually beaten by a plain one with warm-up and cosine decay. If you have budget to tune one thing, tune the rate and its schedule, not the optimiser's name.

The optimiser cannot fix the problemIf the loss will not fall, the cause is almost always unscaled inputs, a broken label pipeline, a missing activation or a learning rate off by two orders of magnitude. Switching optimisers to fix a broken run wastes a day.
In the real worldPublished architectures state their optimiser, rate and schedule precisely, because results do not reproduce without them. When you borrow an architecture, borrow the whole training recipe — swapping in your favourite optimiser is one of the most common reasons a reimplementation underperforms its paper.

Course / Module 3 / 3.3
Section 3.3 of 8

Weight Initialisation and its Techniques

Training starts from numbers somebody chose, and the choice is not a formality. Start at zero and every unit in a layer stays identical forever. Start too large and the activations saturate before the first update. Start too small and the signal fades to nothing by layer six. The fix is a one-line formula that picks the scale from the width of the layer.

aNot zerosbThe right scalecXavier and He
a

Why not zeros, and why not a constant

Watch · four identical units

Set every weight to zero and every unit in a layer computes the same output — zero. During the backward pass every unit then receives the same gradient, and the update makes them identical again. They remain indistinguishable for the entire run. A layer of 512 units has the representational power of one.

The same argument applies to any constant. It is not zero that is the problem; it is symmetry. Units have to start different in order to become different.

So weights are drawn at random. Biases, interestingly, can start at zero: the weights have already broken the symmetry, and a zero bias is a reasonable neutral starting point. That is what every framework does.

The exception worth knowingSetting the final bias of a binary classifier to log(p/(1−p)) for the base rate — rather than zero — saves the network several hundred steps of learning the obvious. On heavily imbalanced data it measurably helps.
Code lab · Python

Symmetry, demonstrated

Python · step 3 · why you cannot start at zero
def relu(z):              return np.maximum(0, z)
def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True);  e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

def one_step(W1, b1, W2, b2, Xb, Yb, lr=.5):
    z1 = Xb @ W1 + b1;  a1 = relu(z1)
    a2 = softmax(a1 @ W2 + b2)
    dz2 = (a2 - Yb) / len(Xb)
    gW2 = a1.T @ dz2
    dz1 = (dz2 @ W2.T) * (z1 > 0)
    gW1 = Xb.T @ dz1
    return W1 - lr * gW1, W2 - lr * gW2

W1 = np.zeros((64, 4));  W2 = np.zeros((4, 10))
for _ in range(5):
    W1, W2 = one_step(W1, np.zeros(4), W2, np.zeros(10), Xtr[:64], onehot[:64])
print("after 5 steps, the 4 hidden units' incoming weights (first 6 pixels):")
print(W1[:6].T)
print("\nEvery unit is identical, because every unit started identical and")
print("received an identical gradient. Four units doing one unit's job, forever.")

g = np.random.default_rng(0)
W1 = g.normal(0, .1, (64, 4));  W2 = g.normal(0, .1, (4, 10))
for _ in range(5):
    W1, W2 = one_step(W1, np.zeros(4), W2, np.zeros(10), Xtr[:64], onehot[:64])
print("\nwith small random weights instead:")
print(W1[:6].T.round(4))
print("\nDifferent from the start, so different gradients, so different features.")
Output

How to read it

After five updates from zeros, all four hidden units have exactly the same incoming weights — the rows of that printout are identical. With small random weights they are different from the first step and diverge from there. Each unit can now specialise in a different feature, which is the only reason a wide layer is worth anything.

b

The scale is the whole problem

Play · set the starting scale

Random is necessary but not sufficient. Consider what a layer does to the size of the signal. A unit sums n inputs, each multiplied by a weight. If the weights are too large, the sum is large, and after a few layers the activations are enormous — saturating sigmoid or tanh, or exploding through ReLU. If they are too small, the signal shrinks at every layer and the deep layers receive essentially nothing.

The gradients mirror this exactly on the way back, because they are multiplied by the same weights. Too-large weights give exploding gradients; too-small weights give vanishing ones. The goal is for the variance of the activations to stay roughly constant from layer to layer.

For a layer with n inputs, the variance of the weighted sum is about n times the variance of one weight times the variance of one input. To keep that equal to the input variance, you need the weight variance to be about 1/n — so the standard deviation should be 1/√n. The right scale depends on the layer's width, which is why a single fixed number like 0.01 cannot be right for every layer.

Why 2010 was a turning pointNetworks deeper than a few layers were considered untrainable. A large part of the reason was that everyone initialised with a fixed small constant, and the signal died before it reached the end.
Code lab · Python

Ten untrained layers, three scales

Python · step 4 · the scale matters as much as the randomness
def layer_stats(scale_fn, depth=10, width=200, act=np.tanh, seed=1):
    """Push data through `depth` untrained layers; report the spread at each one."""
    gg = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    a = gg.normal(0, 1, (512, width))
    spread = []
    for _ in range(depth):
        W = gg.normal(0, scale_fn(width), (width, width))
        a = act(a @ W)
        spread.append(a.std())
    return spread

schemes = {
    "too small  (σ=0.01)": lambda n: 0.01,
    "too large  (σ=1.0)": lambda n: 1.0,
    "Xavier     (σ=1/√n)": lambda n: np.sqrt(1 / n),
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.0))
for name, fn in schemes.items():
    s = layer_stats(fn)
    ax.plot(range(1, 11), s, "o-", ms=4, label=name)
    print(f"  {name:<22} layer 1 spread {s[0]:.4f} → layer 10 spread {s[-1]:.4f}")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("layer"); ax.set_ylabel("standard deviation of activations")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("what happens to the signal through 10 untrained tanh layers")
print("\nToo small: the signal shrinks away and the deep layers see nothing.")
print("Too large: it saturates and the gradients die. Xavier holds it steady.")
Output
  too small  (σ=0.01)    layer 1 spread 0.1388 → layer 10 spread 0.0000
  too large  (σ=1.0)     layer 1 spread 0.9718 → layer 10 spread 0.9705
  Xavier     (σ=1/√n)    layer 1 spread 0.6278 → layer 10 spread 0.2287

Too small: the signal shrinks away and the deep layers see nothing.
Too large: it saturates and the gradients die. Xavier holds it steady.
How to read it

On a log axis the three behaviours are unmistakable. σ = 0.01 falls off a cliff — by layer ten the activations are numerically negligible. σ = 1.0 saturates tanh immediately and the spread pins near its maximum, where the slope is zero. The 1/√n line stays flat across all ten layers, which is exactly the property you want.

c

Xavier and He

Play · pick the scheme

Xavier / Glorot (2010)

σ = √(1/n), or in its symmetric form √(2/(n_in + n_out)), which balances the forward signal against the backward one. Derived for activations that are symmetric around zero and roughly linear near it — tanh and sigmoid. It is still the right default for those, and for a linear output layer.

He / Kaiming (2015)

σ = √(2/n). The derivation is the same with one extra observation: ReLU sets about half its inputs to zero, which halves the variance passing through. Doubling the starting variance compensates exactly — that is the entire origin of the 2.

The ratio between the two is √2 ≈ 1.414, which sounds negligible. Compounded over twenty layers it is a factor of over a thousand, which is the difference between a network that trains and one that does not.

In practice

  • ReLU family → He. This is the default in PyTorch and an explicit option in Keras.
  • tanh / sigmoid → Xavier. Keras's glorot_uniform default.
  • Biases → zeros.
  • Transfer learning → neither. Someone else's trained weights beat any initialisation scheme, every time.
Batch normalisation reduces the stakesSection 3.6 re-standardises the signal at every layer anyway, which makes a network far less sensitive to how it started. It does not make initialisation irrelevant — it makes getting it wrong survivable.
Code lab · Python

Where the √2 comes from

Python · step 5 · He initialisation, for ReLU
for width in (64, 256, 1024):
    xavier, he = np.sqrt(1 / width), np.sqrt(2 / width)
    print(f"  fan-in {width:>5}:  Xavier σ = {xavier:.4f}   He σ = {he:.4f}   (ratio {he/xavier:.3f})")
print("\nReLU sets about half its inputs to zero, halving the variance each layer.")
print("He initialisation doubles the starting variance to compensate — the √2.")

g2 = np.random.default_rng(2)
a_x = a_h = g2.normal(0, 1, (512, 256))
for _ in range(8):
    a_x = relu(a_x @ g2.normal(0, np.sqrt(1 / 256), (256, 256)))
    a_h = relu(a_h @ g2.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / 256), (256, 256)))
print(f"\nafter 8 ReLU layers — Xavier: spread {a_x.std():.2e}   He: spread {a_h.std():.2e}")
Output
  fan-in    64:  Xavier σ = 0.1250   He σ = 0.1768   (ratio 1.414)
  fan-in   256:  Xavier σ = 0.0625   He σ = 0.0884   (ratio 1.414)
  fan-in  1024:  Xavier σ = 0.0312   He σ = 0.0442   (ratio 1.414)

ReLU sets about half its inputs to zero, halving the variance each layer.
He initialisation doubles the starting variance to compensate — the √2.

after 8 ReLU layers — Xavier: spread 5.03e-02   He: spread 1.02e+00
How to read it

The ratio is exactly √2 at every width. The experiment below it is the point: after eight ReLU layers, Xavier's signal has shrunk by a factor of twenty while He's is still the size it started. Each individual layer loses only a little — but layers compound, and that is the whole story of deep network initialisation.

In the real worldYou will usually get this for free, because frameworks default to He for ReLU layers. It becomes your problem the moment you write a custom layer, port weights between frameworks, or initialise from a saved file with the wrong shape convention — all of which produce a model that trains, slowly, to a worse result, with no error message.

Course / Module 3 / 3.4
Section 3.4 of 8

Regularisation

Module 2 ended with a network at 100% on its training data and 98% on data it had not seen. The missing two points are not a failure of capacity — they are the consequence of it. Regularisation is the deliberate act of making the model worse at fitting the training set, in exchange for it fitting everything else better.

aThe bargainbL2 and L1cEarly stoppingdMore data, cheaply
a

The bargain

Play · how much constraint

A model that memorises has to produce a very contorted function — one that passes exactly through every training point, including the noise. Contorted functions need large weights, because a small weight cannot produce a sharp turn.

So: penalise large weights. Add a term to the loss that grows with the size of the weights, and let the optimiser find the compromise. It will fit the data where fitting is worth the penalty, and give up where it is not — which is precisely on the noise.

total loss = prediction loss + λ · (size of the weights)

λ sets the exchange rate. Zero is no constraint; too large and the model is smoothed into uselessness. It is a hyperparameter, which means it is chosen on a validation set — never on the test set, and never by eye on the training curve.

Under-fitting is a failure tooRegularisation pushes towards simpler models, and past a point simpler means wrong. If training and validation accuracy are both falling as you increase λ, you have gone too far — and that is easier to do than people expect.
Code lab · Python

One network, every option as a switch

So that the rest of this module can change one thing at a time and measure it. Note the three-way split in the setup above: anything tuned here is tuned on Xval, and the test set stays untouched until section 3.8.

Python · step 6 · one network definition, every option switchable
def init(sizes, scheme="he", seed=0):
    gg = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = []
    for a_, b_ in zip(sizes, sizes[1:]):
        sd = {"he": np.sqrt(2 / a_), "xavier": np.sqrt(1 / a_), "naive": 0.05}[scheme]
        out.append([gg.normal(0, sd, (a_, b_)), np.zeros(b_)])
    return out

def forward(params, Xb, drop=0.0, gen=None, train=False):
    cache = {"a0": Xb}
    a = Xb
    for i, (W, b) in enumerate(params, 1):
        z = a @ W + b
        if i < len(params):
            a = relu(z)
            if train and drop:
                mask = (gen.random(a.shape) > drop) / (1 - drop)   # inverted dropout
                a = a * mask
                cache[f"m{i}"] = mask
        else:
            a = softmax(z)
        cache[f"z{i}"], cache[f"a{i}"] = z, a
    return a, cache

def backward(params, cache, Yb, l2=0.0, drop=0.0):
    L, n = len(params), len(Yb)
    grads = [None] * L
    dz = (cache[f"a{L}"] - Yb) / n
    for i in range(L, 0, -1):
        W = params[i - 1][0]
        grads[i - 1] = [cache[f"a{i-1}"].T @ dz + l2 * W, dz.sum(axis=0)]
        if i > 1:
            da = dz @ W.T
            if drop:
                da = da * cache[f"m{i-1}"]
            dz = da * (cache[f"z{i-1}"] > 0)
    return grads

def train(l2=0.0, drop=0.0, opt="sgd", epochs=120, lr=0.3, scheme="he", seed=0, hidden=64):
    """Train on Xfit, watch Xval, keep the weights from the best validation epoch."""
    params = init([64, hidden, 10], scheme, seed)
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed + 1)
    state = [[np.zeros_like(W), np.zeros_like(W), np.zeros_like(b), np.zeros_like(b)]
             for W, b in params]
    t = 0
    hist = {"train": [], "val": []}
    best = (0.0, None, 0)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        order = gen.permutation(len(Xfit))
        for s in range(0, len(Xfit), 64):
            idx = order[s:s + 64]
            t += 1
            _, cache = forward(params, Xfit[idx], drop, gen, train=True)
            for k, (gW, gb) in enumerate(backward(params, cache, onehot[idx], l2, drop)):
                if opt == "sgd":
                    params[k][0] -= lr * gW;  params[k][1] -= lr * gb
                else:                                           # adam
                    st = state[k]
                    st[0] = .9 * st[0] + .1 * gW;  st[1] = .999 * st[1] + .001 * gW ** 2
                    st[2] = .9 * st[2] + .1 * gb;  st[3] = .999 * st[3] + .001 * gb ** 2
                    params[k][0] -= lr * (st[0] / (1 - .9 ** t)) / (np.sqrt(st[1] / (1 - .999 ** t)) + 1e-8)
                    params[k][1] -= lr * (st[2] / (1 - .9 ** t)) / (np.sqrt(st[3] / (1 - .999 ** t)) + 1e-8)
        hist["train"].append(accuracy_score(yfit, forward(params, Xfit)[0].argmax(1)))
        va = accuracy_score(yval, forward(params, Xval)[0].argmax(1))
        hist["val"].append(va)
        if va > best[0]:                      # early stopping, kept rather than acted on
            best = (va, copy.deepcopy(params), ep)
    hist["best_epoch"], hist["best_val"] = best[2], best[0]
    return best[1], hist


print("one forward, one backward, with dropout and L2 as switches:")
p = init([64, 64, 10])
probs, c = forward(p, Xtr[:32], drop=.3, gen=np.random.default_rng(0), train=True)
gr = backward(p, c, onehot[:32], l2=1e-3, drop=.3)
print("  output", probs.shape, " gradients", [tuple(x[0].shape) for x in gr])
Output
one forward, one backward, with dropout and L2 as switches:
  output (32, 10)  gradients [(64, 64), (64, 10)]
b

L2, L1, and what each one does to the weights

Play · compare the two penalties

L2 — ridge, or weight decay

Add λ·Σw² to the loss. Its gradient is 2λw, so every step shrinks every weight by a fraction of itself — hence "decay". The shrinkage is proportional, so large weights are pulled hard and small ones barely at all. Nothing is ever driven exactly to zero; the result is many small weights and a smooth function. This is the default, and the one to reach for first.

L1 — lasso

Add λ·Σ|w|. Its gradient is λ·sign(w) — a constant pull of the same size regardless of how small the weight already is. So small weights get pushed all the way to exactly zero and stay there. The result is sparse: most weights are zero and a few are substantial.

The geometric version of the same fact is worth carrying around. Draw the contours of the penalty in two dimensions: Σw² gives circles, Σ|w| gives a diamond with its corners on the axes. Now expand the contours of the prediction loss — ellipses — until they first touch the penalty region. An ellipse meeting a circle touches at an arbitrary point, both coordinates non-zero. An ellipse meeting a diamond very often touches at a corner, and a corner is a point where one coordinate is exactly zero. The corners are why L1 selects.

In a neural network a weight driven to zero is a connection removed. L1 does not merely shrink the model, it prunes the graph — and in the extreme it can leave a unit with nothing feeding it at all.

  • Use L2 when you want a smoother model, which is nearly always.
  • Use L1 when you want feature selection — the surviving non-zero weights tell you which inputs mattered — or when sparsity itself is useful for compression.
  • The usual argument for L1 does not apply here. Lasso is popular in linear regression because dropping terms makes the equation readable. A network with half its weights zeroed is not readable either way, so that benefit vanishes and L2 — which tends to predict slightly better — wins by default.
  • Elastic net is both, with a mixing parameter, and is mostly a tabular-ML technique.
Do not penalise the biasesA bias does not multiply an input, so it cannot make the function sharper. Shrinking it only prevents the layer from shifting its output, which is a restriction with no upside. Frameworks exclude biases by default; hand-written code often forgets.
Code lab · Python

L2 on the digit network

Python · step 7 · weight decay, and what it does to the weights
base_p, base_h = train()
l2_p, l2_h = train(l2=2e-3)
for name, p_, h_ in [("no regularisation", base_p, base_h), ("L2, λ = 0.002", l2_p, l2_h)]:
    norm = np.sqrt(sum((W ** 2).sum() for W, _ in p_))
    print(f"  {name:<20} train {h_['train'][-1]:.2%}  best val {h_['best_val']:.2%}  "
          f"gap {h_['train'][-1]-h_['best_val']:.2%}  ‖W‖ {norm:.2f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
ax.hist(np.concatenate([W.ravel() for W, _ in base_p]), bins=80, alpha=.65, label="no regularisation")
ax.hist(np.concatenate([W.ravel() for W, _ in l2_p]), bins=80, alpha=.65, label="L2")
ax.set_xlabel("weight value"); ax.set_ylabel("count"); ax.legend(fontsize=9)
ax.set_title("L2 pulls every weight towards zero, every step")
Output
  no regularisation    train 100.00%  best val 97.41%  gap 2.59%  ‖W‖ 18.40
  L2, λ = 0.002        train 99.81%  best val 97.41%  gap 2.41%  ‖W‖ 13.16
How to read it

The weight norm falls from about 18 to about 13 and the histogram visibly narrows — L2 is doing exactly what it says. The accuracy barely moves, and that is an honest result worth sitting with: this dataset is small, clean and nearly saturated, so there is very little overfitting left for L2 to remove. On a large, messy problem the same λ can be worth several points.

In the real worldλ is tuned on a log scale — 1e-5, 1e-4, 1e-3 — never linearly. And if you are using Adam, use AdamW, which applies the decay correctly rather than running it through the adaptive denominator.
c

Early stopping

Play · when do you stop?

The cheapest regularisation there is, and frequently the most effective. Watch the validation loss each epoch. It falls, reaches a minimum, and starts climbing while the training loss keeps falling — that turning point is where the model switches from learning to memorising. Keep the weights from that epoch; discard everything after.

Doing it properly

  • Patience. Do not stop the first epoch the validation loss rises — it is noisy. Wait for 5 or 10 epochs with no improvement.
  • Restore the best weights, not the last ones. Stopping at epoch 40 and keeping epoch 40's weights when epoch 30 was the best is a common and silent mistake.
  • Validate on a set that is not the test set. The epoch is a hyperparameter like any other; choosing it on the test set makes the test score meaningless.

Why it works as regularisation: the weights grow over training, and stopping early is, loosely, a way of limiting how large they get — a less precise, much cheaper version of what L2 does deliberately.

Always onIt costs one extra evaluation per epoch and a copy of the weights. There is no argument against it, and EarlyStopping(restore_best_weights=True) belongs in every training script you write.
d

More data, without more data

Play · one digit, many versions

Overfitting is a ratio between model capacity and data. Every other technique here reduces the numerator. Augmentation raises the denominator — by generating new training examples from the ones you have, using transformations that should not change the label.

A 7 rotated by five degrees is still a 7. A photo of a cat mirrored left-to-right is still a cat. If the model is forced to get both right, it has to learn something about the shape rather than the pixels.

What it actually prevents

Suppose one training image of a 7 happens to carry a stray dot in its top-left corner, and no other image in the set has a mark there. The network has thousands of weights and one instruction: fit the data. It is entirely plausible that some part of it settles on dot in the top-left corner ⇒ 7, because across the whole training set that rule is never once wrong. It is also nonsense, and it fails the moment a 3 arrives with a speck of ink.

Now augment. Add noise to every image and 3s and 8s acquire corner specks too; rotate, and the dot moves elsewhere. The correlation the network was about to exploit is destroyed before it can be learned. Augmentation does not only add data — it breaks the accidental regularities that every small sample contains.

  • Images: small rotations, shifts, zooms, horizontal flips, brightness and contrast jitter, random crops. Mixup and CutMix blend pairs of images and their labels.
  • Audio: time stretching, pitch shift, background noise, masking spans of the spectrogram.
  • Text: synonym substitution, back-translation through another language, random deletion.
  • Tabular: hardest — there is rarely a transformation that provably preserves the label. SMOTE interpolates between minority-class rows, with care.

Augmentation and oversampling

The same mechanism, two different purposes, and the names are worth keeping straight. Oversampling duplicates or synthesises examples of a minority class to correct a 90/10 imbalance. Augmentation generates variants of every example to combat overfitting. Both make data from data; only the motive differs.

The label must survive the transformationFlipping a photo of a cat is fine. Flipping a 2 gives something that is not a digit at all, and flipping a 6 gives a 9 — with a label that still says 6. Vertical flips are standard for satellite imagery and catastrophic for handwriting. The valid set of augmentations is a property of your data, not a library default.
In the real worldFor images, augmentation is usually worth more than every other regularisation technique combined, and costs only CPU time while the GPU is busy. It is also the only one of these that encodes actual domain knowledge — which transformations preserve meaning is something you know and the model does not. At the far end of the same idea, teams now generate training data outright: GANs and diffusion models synthesising faces for a recogniser, and game engines rendering whole virtual streets, in every weather and at every hour, to train driving models on situations too rare or too dangerous to collect.
