Course / Module 3 / 3.5
Section 3.5 of 8

Dropout

On every training batch, pick a random half of the units in a layer and switch them off entirely. It sounds like sabotage and it works remarkably well: the network cannot rely on any particular unit being present, so it is forced to spread what it knows across many of them. The result is redundant, robust features — and a model that is, in effect, an average of thousands of smaller networks.

aThe random maskbWhy it workscScaling, and inferencedWhere to put it
a

The mask

Play · drop rate, and a new mask each batch

During training, for each batch and each dropout layer, draw a fresh random mask: each unit is kept with probability (1−p) and zeroed with probability p. Multiply the layer's activations by the mask. That is the whole forward-pass change.

The backward pass needs the same mask applied to the gradient — a unit that contributed nothing must receive nothing. In code that means remembering the mask between the two passes, exactly like the other cached values from section 2.5.

The mask is different for every batch, so no two batches train the same network. Over an epoch, every unit is dropped many times and kept many times.

Typical rates0.5 for large fully connected hidden layers — the original paper's recommendation, and still a good default. 0.1 to 0.3 for smaller layers, and for convolutional layers, where neighbouring activations are already correlated and dropping single pixels achieves little. On the input layer the usual figure is a keep probability of 0.8, i.e. a drop rate of 0.2 — much gentler, because every feature you drop is information the network can never recover. Modern vision architectures often use none at all, relying on batch norm and augmentation instead.
b

Why breaking the network helps it

Watch · two ways to recognise an 8

Start with a team of four, training together for a competition. Train them as a group every day and something predictable happens: one or two turn out to be strong, they answer everything, and they get stronger — while the other two coast, because nothing ever requires them to contribute. On the day, that team is brittle. Its whole capability rests on two people and one unfamiliar question away from collapse.

Now change the drill. Each day only a random pair turns up. Nobody can rely on the strong one being in the room, so everybody has to learn the geometry. The team ends up slower to train and far harder to break — and on competition day all four show up, each able to do the job.

That is dropout, and there are two ways to say why it works. Both are correct and both are useful.

It prevents co-adaptation

Without dropout, units specialise in ways that depend on each other: unit 7 learns to fire only when unit 12 also fires, because during training unit 12 was always there. That arrangement is fragile — it is tuned to the training set rather than to the problem.

The sharper version of this involves two layers. Suppose a unit in one layer introduces a systematic error, and a unit above it happens to learn to cancel that error. The loss never sees the mistake, so no gradient ever flows back to fix its cause. The pair have co-adapted: together they are correct, individually they are both wrong, and the arrangement only holds for the data they were trained on. Drop the corrector for a batch and the error finally reaches the output — where the gradient can get at the unit that is actually producing it.

It is an ensemble, cheaply

A layer of n units has 2ⁿ possible masks, and each batch trains one of those sub-networks — all sharing the same weights. At prediction time, using all units with the appropriate scaling approximates averaging over all of them. Ensembles reliably beat single models; dropout gets most of that benefit for the cost of one model.

What it costsTraining takes longer to converge — typically 2 to 3 times as many epochs, because each update sees a crippled network. Training loss will also look worse than it really is, since it is measured with units missing. Compare validation numbers, not training ones.
c

The scaling, and what happens at prediction time

Play · with and without the correction

Dropping half the units halves the expected size of the layer's output. The next layer has learned weights suited to that reduced signal. Switch dropout off at prediction time and the next layer suddenly receives twice what it is calibrated for — and the model's outputs are nonsense.

The original fix — now called vanilla dropout — was to multiply the weights by (1−p) at prediction time. Everyone now uses inverted dropout instead: divide by (1−p) during training, immediately after applying the mask. Same arithmetic, moved to where it cannot be forgotten.

The ensemble framing makes the need for it obvious. Train a hundred separate models and you combine them by averaging, not by adding — add them and the result is a hundred times too large. Dropout trains its sub-networks one at a time and then runs them all at once, so the same division has to happen somewhere.

mask = (random(shape) > p) / (1 − p)
a = a * mask

Now the expected output is unchanged during training, and prediction time needs no special handling at all — you simply stop applying the mask. The correction has already been paid for.

The bug this causes in hand-written codeForgetting to disable dropout at inference. The model still produces plausible output, just slightly randomly, and gives a different answer for the same input twice. In PyTorch this is what model.eval() is for, and forgetting it is a rite of passage.
Code lab · Python

Inverted dropout, and its effect on the gap

print("\ninverted dropout — scaled up, so the mean survives:")
print("  mean before", a.mean(), " after", round((a * mask_inv).mean(), 3))
print("\nThat is why nothing special happens at prediction time: the scaling")

drop_p, drop_h = train(drop=0.3)
print()
for name, h_ in [("no regularisation", base_h), ("dropout 0.3", drop_h)]:
    print(f"  {name:<20} train {h_['train'][-1]:.2%}  best val {h_['best_val']:.2%}  gap {h_['train'][-1]-h_['best_val']:.2%}")
Output

That is why nothing special happens at prediction time: the scaling
was already paid for during training. Dropout is simply switched off.

  no regularisation    train 100.00%  best val 97.41%  gap 2.59%
  dropout 0.3          train 100.00%  best val 98.15%  gap 1.85%
How to read it

Naive masking halves the mean; the inverted version leaves it at 1.0, which is the entire point. Below that, dropout at 0.3 lifts validation accuracy from 97.41% to 98.15% and cuts the train-validation gap from 2.59 to 1.85 points — the clearest win any single technique gets on this dataset, and achieved by making the network's job harder.

d

Where to put it

Play · place the dropout layers
  • After the activation of a hidden layer. The standard position: Dense → ReLU → Dropout.
  • Not on the output layer. Randomly zeroing class scores corrupts the prediction for no benefit.
  • On the input layer, gently if at all. A keep probability around 0.8 is the documented recommendation and does work as noise injection — but a dropped input is information destroyed before the network ever sees it, so the rate stays far below what hidden layers take.
  • Heaviest on the widest layers. They have the most capacity and therefore the most to memorise with.
  • With batch norm, carefully. The two interact — dropout changes the variance that batch norm has just standardised. The common convention is Dense → BatchNorm → ReLU → Dropout, and many modern architectures simply use one or the other.
A sensible defaultStart without it. Train, look at the train–validation gap, and add dropout only if there is a gap worth closing. Adding regularisation to a model that is underfitting makes it worse, and people do this constantly because dropout has a reputation for being free.
In the real worldDropout is far less universal than it was. Large vision models use augmentation and batch norm instead; transformers use it at low rates inside attention and feed-forward blocks. It remains the first thing to reach for on a fully connected network trained on modest data — which is a great deal of applied work.
Back · 3.4RegularisationNext · 3.6Batch Normalisation
Course / Module 3 / 3.6
Section 3.6 of 8

Batch Normalisation

Section 1.4 scaled the inputs so the first layer would behave. But layer five's inputs are layer four's outputs, and nobody scaled those — and they keep changing as layer four learns. Batch normalisation applies the same standardisation between every pair of layers, continuously, during training. It is a short piece of arithmetic that made much deeper networks trainable.

aThe shifting targetbThe operationcγ and βdTraining vs serving
a

A target that moves while you aim at it

Play · how deep, with and without

Layer five spends training adapting to the distribution of numbers layer four sends it. But layer four is also learning, so that distribution keeps shifting — its mean drifts, its spread grows or shrinks. Layer five is fitting a moving target, and so is every layer above it. The deeper the network, the worse it compounds: a small change in layer one is amplified through everything after it.

The original paper called this internal covariate shift. Later work argued that the real benefit is something subtler — batch norm smooths the loss surface, making it less sensitive to the learning rate and to initialisation. The explanation is still debated. The effect is not.

And why it regularises

This part is often asserted and rarely explained. Batches are drawn at random, so row 2 lands in a different company every epoch. Its normalised value depends on the mean and variance of whichever other rows happened to share its batch — so row 2 arrives at the next layer as slightly different numbers each time it appears.

Which is data augmentation, arriving by another route. The network cannot latch onto a precise numerical quirk of row 2, because row 2 is never numerically the same twice. The jitter is small and it is enough to make memorising individual examples measurably harder.

It also explains a practical consequence: the regularisation weakens as the batch grows, because a large batch's statistics barely move from one draw to the next.

What it buys you in practice

  • Much higher learning rates become stable, so training is faster.
  • Initialisation matters far less — a bad scale gets corrected at the first normalised layer. With batch norm throughout, careful initialisation and even input scaling become close to unnecessary, though both are still worth doing.
  • Deeper networks train at all. Networks beyond about twenty layers were impractical before it.
  • A mild regularising effect, by a mechanism worth spelling out — see below.
Code lab · Python

Eight layers, with and without

Python · step 9 · normalising between layers
def spread_through(depth=8, width=128, bn=False, seed=3):
    gg = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    a = gg.normal(0, 1, (256, width))
    out = []
    for _ in range(depth):
        a = a @ gg.normal(0, 1.4 * np.sqrt(2 / width), (width, width))   # slightly too large on purpose
        if bn:
            a = (a - a.mean(0)) / (a.std(0) + 1e-8)
        a = relu(a)
        out.append(a.std())
    return out

no_bn, with_bn = spread_through(), spread_through(bn=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
ax.plot(range(1, 9), no_bn, "o-", ms=4, label="without batch norm")
ax.plot(range(1, 9), with_bn, "o-", ms=4, label="with batch norm")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("layer"); ax.set_ylabel("activation spread")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("batch norm re-centres the signal at every layer")
print(f"  without BN: layer 1 {no_bn[0]:.3f} → layer 8 {no_bn[-1]:.3f}  ({no_bn[-1]/no_bn[0]:.1f}×)")
print(f"  with BN:    layer 1 {with_bn[0]:.3f} → layer 8 {with_bn[-1]:.3f}  ({with_bn[-1]/with_bn[0]:.1f}×)")
print("\nWithout it the signal grows layer by layer until the network is unusable.")
print("With it, every layer receives inputs of a predictable size, whatever came before.")
Output
  without BN: layer 1 1.158 → layer 8 9.551  (8.3×)
  with BN:    layer 1 0.584 → layer 8 0.590  (1.0×)

Without it the signal grows layer by layer until the network is unusable.
With it, every layer receives inputs of a predictable size, whatever came before.
How to read it

With weights deliberately set a little too large, the signal grows roughly eightfold over eight layers — and that is with ReLU, which does not saturate. With sigmoid or tanh the network would be dead by layer four. The normalised line is flat: every layer hands on a signal of a predictable size, whatever the layer below it happened to do.

b

The operation itself

Watch · four steps, per feature, per batch

For each feature (each column of the layer's output), across the examples in the current batch:

μ = mean of the batch
σ² = variance of the batch
x̂ = (x − μ) / √(σ² + ε)
y = γ·x̂ + β

The first three lines are ordinary standardisation — exactly what you did to the pixels in section 1.4, applied to a hidden layer and recomputed for every batch. The ε, around 1e-5, guards against a feature that is constant within the batch.

Note that μ and σ are computed per feature across the batch, not per example. Unit 7's statistics come from unit 7's values over all 64 examples. This is why batch norm behaves oddly with very small batches — with a batch of 2, the statistics are noise.

Before or after the activation?

A layer does two things — a weighted sum, then an activation — and the normalisation can go either side. The original paper put it before the activation, which is the more common choice and the one that makes the saturation argument work. Putting it after is also widely used and sometimes trains better. There is no settled answer; follow the architecture you are copying, and if you are choosing from scratch, normalise before the activation.

The whole operation is differentiableμ and σ depend on the inputs, so the backward pass has to differentiate through them too. It is fiddly to derive and entirely mechanical — and it is the reason batch norm has a measurable compute cost, not just a memory one.
c

γ and β: giving the choice back

Play · move the learned parameters

Forcing every layer's output to mean 0 and variance 1 is a strong constraint, and sometimes the wrong one. A sigmoid unit restricted to that range can only ever use the near-linear middle of its curve — you have normalised away its ability to be non-linear.

So batch norm adds two learnable parameters per feature: γ scales the normalised value and β shifts it. The network decides, by gradient descent like everything else, what mean and variance each feature should actually have.

Critically, γ = σ and β = μ recovers the original un-normalised values exactly. The layer can undo the normalisation entirely if that is best. In practice it never does, but having the option is what makes the constraint safe.

A small consequence

Because β already shifts the output, the preceding layer's bias is redundant — it would be subtracted out by the mean step anyway. Frameworks set use_bias=False on a layer followed by batch norm, which saves a few parameters and avoids a pointless degree of freedom.

Layer norm, in passingBatch norm normalises each feature across the batch. Layer norm normalises each example across its features — so it does not depend on the batch at all, works with a batch of 1, and is what transformers and recurrent models use.
d

Training and serving are different

Play · which mode

At training time the statistics come from the current batch. At prediction time that is unusable — a single request has no batch, and even if it did, the prediction for one input would depend on which other inputs arrived alongside it. That is not acceptable behaviour for a model.

So during training the layer also maintains a running average of the means and variances it has seen, updated each batch with a momentum term around 0.99. At inference it uses those frozen statistics instead. Batch norm becomes a fixed affine transformation — two multiplications and an addition — and can be folded into the preceding layer's weights entirely.

Evaluating on a test set is the one case where you have a choice, because there you do have the whole set at once. Running the test set as a single batch and using its own statistics gives the most directly comparable number against training. Using the frozen running averages gives the number you will actually see in production, one request at a time. They are answers to different questions, and the second is the one to quote.

The failure modes

  • Forgetting to switch modes. Serving in training mode makes predictions depend on batch composition; the model gives different answers to the same input. model.eval() in PyTorch.
  • Too few batches before the running averages settle. A model trained for ten steps has meaningless inference statistics.
  • Very small batches. With a batch of 2 or 4 the per-batch statistics are mostly noise, and training becomes unstable. Use group norm or layer norm instead.
  • A distribution shift after deployment. The frozen statistics describe the training data. If live data drifts, they are wrong and nothing warns you.
Why this is worth knowing preciselyA batch-norm model that scores well offline and badly in production, with no code change between them, is nearly always one of these four. It is among the most common and least obvious deployment bugs in deep learning.
In the real worldFolding batch norm into the preceding convolution is a standard inference optimisation — it removes the layer entirely at serving time with no change in output. Every mobile and edge deployment toolkit does it automatically.

Course / Module 3 / 3.7
Section 3.7 of 8

Types of Neural Networks

Everything so far has been a fully connected network: every unit sees every unit below it. That makes no assumption about the input, which is both its virtue and its weakness — an image has structure a dense layer throws away. Each major family is, at heart, a different assumption about what the input is, built into the architecture so the network does not have to learn it.

aSix familiesbWeight sharingcChoosing
a

Six families

Play · pick a family

They are not rivals so much as different starting assumptions, and real systems combine them freely — a convolutional encoder feeding a recurrent decoder, a transformer over patches of an image.

The split that actually matters

Before the six, there are two. A feed-forward network passes information in one direction only: layer to layer to output, with nothing fed back. A recurrent network feeds its own previous output back in as part of the next input, which is how it carries a memory.

Everything you have built in this course is feed-forward — and so is a convolutional network. A CNN is not an alternative to feed-forward; it is a feed-forward network whose layers are arranged as grids and whose weights are shared. Keeping that straight saves a lot of confusion later.

And "deep" means?Nothing precise. A deep neural network is one with many layers, and nobody agrees on many: some would say more than three, others reserve it for fourteen or more. In a recurrent network, where the same cell is reapplied, counting layers stops being well defined at all. It is a description, not a category.
  • Dense / MLP. No assumption. Right for tabular data and as the head on top of something else.
  • Convolutional. Assumes the input is a grid where nearby things relate, and that a useful pattern is useful anywhere in it. Images, spectrograms, and 1-D signals.
  • Recurrent (LSTM, GRU). Assumes an ordered sequence of unknown length, processed one step at a time while carrying a memory.
  • Autoencoder. Learns to reconstruct its own input through a narrow middle, so the middle has to be a compressed description. No labels needed.
  • GAN. Two networks in competition — one generating samples, one judging them. Generation rather than prediction.
  • Transformer. Every position attends to every other position directly, with order supplied separately. No recurrence, so it parallelises, which is why it scaled.
b

What weight sharing buys

Play · image size

The single most important idea behind convolutional networks is not the convolution — it is that the same small set of weights is reused at every position.

A dense layer taking a 28 × 28 image to 128 units needs 100,480 parameters, and every one of them is specific to a particular pixel. A detector for a vertical edge learned at the top-left is useless at the bottom-right; the network must learn it again, separately, from separate examples.

A convolutional layer learns one 3 × 3 window — nine numbers per channel — and slides it across the whole image. Three consequences follow:

  • Parameters do not grow with image size. The same filter works on 28 × 28 and on 4K.
  • Translation equivariance. A pattern learned anywhere is recognised everywhere, which is free generalisation rather than learned generalisation.
  • Far less overfitting, because far fewer parameters are chasing the same data.

Recurrent networks share weights the same way, but across time rather than space: the same cell is applied at every step, which is what lets one model handle sequences of any length.

The general principleIf your data has a symmetry — translation, time, rotation, permutation — an architecture that builds it in will beat one that has to learn it, especially when data is scarce. Architecture is how you tell the model what you already know.
Code lab · Python

Python · step 10 · dense vs convolutional, by parameter count
h = w = 28

    ("Conv 3×3, 32 → 64 channels", 3 * 3 * 32 * 64 + 64),
    ("Dense 784 → 784 (same size out)", 784 * 784 + 784),
]:
    print(f"  {name:<34} {params:>9,} parameters")
print("\nA convolution learns one small window and slides it over the whole image,")
print("so the parameter count does not grow with the image. It also keeps the grid,")
print("which a dense layer throws away the moment you flatten.")
Output
  Dense 784 → 128                      100,480 parameters
  Conv 3×3, 1 → 32 channels                320 parameters
  Conv 3×3, 32 → 64 channels            18,496 parameters
  Dense 784 → 784 (same size out)      615,440 parameters

A convolution learns one small window and slides it over the whole image,
so the parameter count does not grow with the image. It also keeps the grid,
which a dense layer throws away the moment you flatten.
How to read it

A 3 × 3 convolution producing 32 channels costs 320 parameters. The dense layer doing a roughly comparable job costs 100,480 — over three hundred times more, for a worse result, because it also discarded the knowledge of which pixels are adjacent. This is the whole argument, in four lines of arithmetic.

c

Choosing one

Play · what does your input look like?

Work from the data, not from what is fashionable.

  • Rows and columns of mixed types — dense network, and genuinely consider gradient-boosted trees first. On tabular data they still frequently win.
  • Images — convolutional, or a vision transformer if you have a great deal of data or a pretrained model. Start from pretrained weights almost always.
  • Text — a pretrained transformer. Training one from scratch is not a sensible use of anyone's budget.
  • Time series — try classical methods first, then 1-D convolutions, then recurrent or transformer models. Simple baselines are embarrassingly strong here.
  • Audio — convert to a spectrogram and treat it as an image, which is what most systems do.
  • No labels — autoencoder for compression or anomaly detection; self-supervised pretraining if you have scale.

And the advice that overrides all of it: use somebody else's trained weights. Fine-tuning a pretrained model on a few thousand examples beats training a bespoke architecture on them, nearly every time, for a fraction of the effort.

Architecture is the last thing to tuneIn applied work, better data, better labels and a sensible baseline move the number far more than the choice of family. The architecture question is interesting; it is rarely the bottleneck.
In the real worldA clinic automating appointment reminders needs a dense model on ten tabular columns, or a rule. The same clinic reading X-rays needs a pretrained convolutional network fine-tuned on its own scans. Recognising which problem is in front of you is worth more than knowing any single architecture in depth.

Course / Module 3 / 3.8
Section 3.8 of 8 · Hands-on

Putting It Together

Every block from this module, applied to the digit classifier one change at a time, with a three-way split so that the final number means something. The result is an honest one: the techniques help, by about a point, and understanding why it is only a point is worth more than the point.

aThe splitbOne change at a timecThe scoreboarddA checklist
a

Why three splits, not two

Play · how many things did you try?

Module 2 used two splits, and that was fine: there was nothing to choose. Module 3 adds a learning rate, a λ, a dropout rate, a width, an optimiser and a stopping epoch. Every one of those is selected by trying options and keeping the best — and "the best on set X" is an optimistic estimate of performance on set X, because you chose it for scoring well there.

Try twenty configurations and keep the winner, and you have partly selected for whichever one got lucky on that particular sample. The reported number is inflated by an amount nobody can measure afterwards.

So: fit on one set, choose on a second, report on a third that was never consulted. The test set is read once, at the very end, and the number you get is the one you quote.

Cross-validation, when data is scarceSplitting three ways is expensive on a small dataset. K-fold cross-validation reuses the data by rotating which fold is held out — more compute, far less waste, and the standard answer below a few thousand rows.
b

One change at a time

Watch · the discipline

Change five things, improve by a point, and you know nothing. You cannot tell which change helped, whether two of them cancelled, or whether one actively hurt and the others carried it. The next time you face a similar problem you have learned nothing transferable.

So change one thing per run, against a fixed baseline, with the same seed. It is slower and it is the only way the results mean anything.

The order that usually works

  1. Get it to overfit first. A model that cannot reach high training accuracy has a bug or is too small. Fix that before adding anything that holds it back.
  2. Then add regularisation, one technique at a time, watching the validation gap.
  3. Then tune the optimiser and schedule.
  4. Then, and only then, read the test set.
Seeds matter more than you want them toOn a small dataset, two runs differing only in random seed can differ by half a point. Before celebrating a 0.3-point improvement, run both configurations three times and compare the spread.
c

The scoreboard

Compare · every configuration

Test accuracy. The test set was read once, after every other decision had been made on the validation set.

The honest reading of these numbers:

  • Dropout is the clear winner here, taking validation from 97.4% to 98.2% and cutting the train–validation gap from 2.6 points to 1.9. It is the one technique attacking the actual problem — a model with enough capacity to memorise 1,077 examples.
  • L2 does almost nothing to the score, while visibly shrinking the weights. It is working; there is simply not much overfitting left for it to remove once the gap is under three points.
  • Adam converges faster but does not finish higher. On a problem this small, plain SGD has ample time to arrive anyway. Adam earns its keep on large models and tight compute budgets.
  • Wider is not better. 128 units with no extra regularisation scores slightly below 64.

The number is not the win

Read the gap column rather than the accuracy column. The plain network scored 98.0% with a 2.6-point spread between what it knew about its training data and what it knew in general — it had memorised the first and was coasting on the second. The regularised one scores 98.4% with a 1.8-point spread. The accuracy moved by four tenths of a point; the evidence that the model learned rather than memorised improved a great deal more.

That distinction matters because of what each number predicts. Accuracy on 450 digits is a noisy estimate of accuracy on 450 more. A closed train–validation gap is a statement that the model is not relying on accidents of the sample — which is what survives contact with data drawn a year later, from a different scanner, in a different hand.

The ceiling is the rest of the story. Eight of 450 test digits are misread, and at 8 × 8 several of those are genuinely ambiguous. A technique cannot recover accuracy the data does not contain.

Where these techniques actually payNot here. On a 50-layer network, a million images and a week of GPU time, initialisation decides whether training starts at all, batch norm decides whether it is stable, augmentation is worth several points, and the optimiser decides whether it finishes this week. This dataset is a laboratory for understanding them, not a demonstration of their value.

How to read it

Read the val column to compare configurations — that is the column every decision was based on. The TEST column is the estimate of real performance, and the fact that it sits slightly above validation for most rows is ordinary sampling variation on 450 examples, not a sign of anything. The gap column is the thing this module set out to close, and it fell from 2.59 to 1.76.

d

A checklist to keep

Play · what is going wrong?

Before training

  • Inputs scaled, with the scaling computed on the training split only.
  • He initialisation for ReLU, Xavier for tanh, zeros for biases.
  • Output activation and loss matched: softmax with cross-entropy, sigmoid with binary cross-entropy, nothing with squared error.
  • A baseline measured and written down.
  • Three splits, and the test set put away.

While training

  • Adam at 0.001, or SGD with momentum 0.9 and a rate you searched for.
  • Mini-batches of 32 to 256.
  • Both losses plotted from the first epoch.
  • Early stopping on validation, restoring the best weights.
  • Overfit deliberately first, then regularise.

Before shipping

  • Dropout and batch norm switched to inference mode.
  • Scaling constants saved with the weights, in the same artefact.
  • A confusion matrix, not just an accuracy figure.
  • The misclassified examples looked at, by a person.
Where to go nextConvolutional networks for images, recurrent models and transformers for sequences, and — before any of those — transfer learning, which will beat anything you train from scratch on a modest dataset. Everything in this course is still running underneath all three.
In the real worldAlmost every deep-learning failure in production traces back to this checklist rather than to anything exotic: unscaled inputs, a mismatched loss, inference mode left on training, scaling constants that drifted, or a test set that was quietly tuned against. The architecture is rarely the problem.
